analytic.title: Morphological adjustments of the Yamuna River in the Himalayan foothills in response to natural and anthropogenic stresses

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Rivers can adjust to natural and anthropogenic stresses through changes in flow regime and sediment dynamics. Flow regulation due to dam construction can modify sediment transport processes, causing morphological adjustments and changes in conveyance capacity. In this study, we explored morphological adjustments along a 46 km segment of the Yamuna River in the Himalayan foothills from Dakpathar Barrage to Hathni Kund Barrage using a combination of remote sensing approaches. The cloud computing platform Google Earth Engine (GEE) was used to analyze multi-temporal collections of Landsat satellite imagery acquired between 1989 and 2021. Active river channels (including water and exposed sediment) were classified using an MNDWI and NDVI thresholding approach from annually resolved temporal composite images. Declassified CORONA satellite imagery (acquired in 1965, 1973, and 1976) was manually digitized to provide longer-term insights into channel change. Morphological adjustments were assessed using the RivMAP toolbox, providing quantitative information on the rates of bank erosion and accretion, bank line shifts, and changes in active channel width.

Results showed a substantial narrowing of the active channel after 2013, which coincided with the construction of the Lakhwar-Vyasi Dam. We calculated a 67% reduction in mean active channel width, narrowing from ~800 m in 1989 to ~250 m in 2021. During the same period, evidence of sand mining in the active channel indicates a substantial increase in mining activities after 2015. The concept of stasis was explored under different flow regulation scenarios to suggest that the river has undergone a state of inactivity, where the river is doing nothing for much longer durations. We suggest that the combined effects of flow regulation and increased mining activities during the same period have altered river morphology, and further stresses due to a combination of human activities can be damaging for the river regime.
This study sheds light on the potential implications of multiple stresses acting on the Yamuna River at the same time, which can inform future sustainable river management activities.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Sediment dynamics across the Earth's surface are of primary importance for understanding the redistribution of the Earth's mass over thousands of years. Sediment transport from uplands to lowlands can shape landscapes over shorter timescales than tectonic activity and uplift (Korup, 2012). Large rivers originating from the high mountains are efficient conveyors of sediment (Syvitski et al., 2022;Wang et al., 2011), and influence river morphology, planform, grain size, bedforms, and various other river characteristics (Ashmore, 2013;Church, 2006;Latrubesse, 2008). Extreme flood events are major drivers of morphological change in rivers (Hauer and Habersack, 2009;Magilligan et al., 2015), and sediment mobilised during extreme floods, together with the instream erosion and deposition, drive changes in river planform (Borga et al., 2019;Pasternack and Wyrick, 2017). However, specific geomorphic changes depend on the flood hydrograph, sediment flux, geologic formation, topography, valley confinement, and various other controls (Brogan et al., 2017;Lane et al., 2017;Wohl et al., 2019). Any changes in upstream sediment production due to natural and anthropogenic stresses (Best and Darby, 2020) may be reflected in the flow regime, sediment dynamics, and morphological regime in downstream reaches (Jain and Sinha, 2004;Meybeck and Vörösmarty, 2005;Wheaton et al., 2013).

In recent years, there have been substantial increases in the construction of dams, levees, and other water structures globally to address the rising demands of food, water, and energy. More than 3700 hydropower dams (>1 MW) are either planned or operating globally (Zarfl et al., 2015), with Asia the hotspot of hydropower dam construction with 23.85 GW of new capacity installed in 2021, reaching a global hydropower capacity of 1360 GW (IHA, 2022). Dams and barrages may trap a significant proportion of sediment upstream causing the downstream reaches to be sediment starved, having serious implications on the morphological regime including the shrinkage of deltas (Schmidt and Wilcock, 2008;Syvitski et al., 2009;Vörösmarty et al., 2003). Quantifying the effects of dam construction on sediment flux from 2003 to 2017, the Madeira Dam Complex in the Amazon basin has resulted in a 30% net reduction in the suspended sediment concentration at Porto Velho on the Mediera River (Ayes Rivera et al., 2019), while the Three Gorges Reservoir on the Yangtze River caused a net reduction of 98.7% in the mean annual sediment deposition in Lake Dongting (Zhou et al., 2016). In India, the Brahmani, Godavari, and Mahanadi Rivers have shown a 50%, 40%, and 74%, net reduction in sediment delivered to river deltas respectively, due to upstream damming over the last 50 years (Syvitski et al., 2009). In contrast, ground clearance and mining activities may increase sediment production causing increased sediment flow, as has occurred on the Fly River in Papua New Guinea (Walling, 2006).

Focusing on rivers with source areas in the high Himalayas, sediment eroded from the mountains are flushed into the Indo-Gangetic plains, forming one of the most fertile (doab region) alluvial regions of the world. However, Himalayan rivers have been highly regulated in recent years to increase hydropower capacity, water storage, and flood mitigation (Bandyopadhyay, 2002;Grill et al., 2019). In 2021, India installed 803 MW of new hydropower capacity, ranking third after China, and Canada (IHA, 2022). Currently the Ganga River is regulated by six dams upstream of Rishikesh, and 37 new dams are planned in the Upper Ganga Basin (UGB) (Swarnkar et al., 2021;Zarfl et al., 2015). Milliman and Syvitski (1992) showed that Himalayan rivers like the Ganga have been impacted by anthropogenic interventions, suggesting a decline in sediment load by nearly 50% (Walling and Fang, 2003). Additionally, river sediment is widely used as a construction material in India, attracting illegal sand mining and gravel quarrying, which may pose threats to river ecology (Das, 2014). Moreover, Himalayan rivers are highly sensitive to anthropogenic or climatic alterations (Mishra and Lilhare, 2016). A recent study on the Ganga river has shown an increase in the frequency of extreme events, probably due to an increase in rainfall and the construction of dams and barrages (Swarnkar et al., 2021), however, the impacts on river morphology as the river exits the Himalayas remains relatively unknown. The Yamuna River, a major tributary of the Ganga, serves the hydropower, drinking water, and irrigation needs of the north Indian community.

The river has been regulated in recent decades with the construction of the largest hydropower dam on the Yamuna River 30.5208 N,77.9144 E, gross storage capacity: 580 Mm 3 ). In addition to this, sediment mining along the Yamuna River is considerable (Singh and Kumar, 2018), which may have serious impacts on the river morphology. The combined effect of flow regulation and increased sediment mining may have severe implications for river morphology and requires scientific attention.

By affecting flow regime and sediment dynamics, anthropogenic stresses may enable the river to do nothing for much longer durations, relating to the concept of stasis: a state of complete inactivity. In sedimentation systems, stasis can be defined as a state when neither erosion nor deposition is occurring, unlike equilibrium (static or dynamic), where erosion/deposition is either constant or fluctuates around a mean value (Straub and Foreman, 2018;Tipper, 2015Tipper, , 2016)). In river systems, stasis is a condition of the constant morphological regime as a result of the cessation of erosion and deposition. For floodplain dominated rivers, the ratio of floodplain width to channel-belt width is usually 20:1, and the ratio of channel-belt width to the channel is typically 4:1 (Bridge, 2003). This comprises nearly 95%, 4%, and 1% of the area of the river system for the floodplain (excluding channel belt and channel), channel-belt (excluding channel), and 1% area for the channel itself (Tipper, 2015), where erosion/deposition can occur. Sedimentation in floodplains and the channel belt only occurs during floods, and only in areas where sediment can be reached in suspension. Further , Tipper, (2015) presented a first order estimate of stasis for unregulated rivers, showing that 98% of the time a river system remain in stasis. However, flow regulation from dams even further reduces the probability of flooding in the floodplain and channel belt, shifting the river to stasis for longer durations.

Global satellite data and semi-automated processing techniques offer new opportunities for geomorphological analyses (Fryirs et al., 2019). Multi-temporal satellite data allow lateral channel dynamics to be assessed for rivers with considerable geomorphic adjustment (Wang and Xu, 2018). The temporal range of satellite data available is now sufficient to detect channel response to environmental drivers in responsive rivers (Piégay et al., 2020). Multi-spectral indices calculated from satellite data enables features of interest to be identified in fluvial systems (Spada et al., 2018), including discrete riverscape units (e.g., water channel and unvegetated sediment bars). Advanced satellite data processing tools, including cloud-based computing platforms such as Google Earth Engine (GEE), provide an opportunity to apply satellite data analyses at unprecedented spatial and temporal scales (Gorelick et al., 2017).

Satellite-derived outputs can be with coupled with semi-automated analysis tools that measure planform statistics (e.g., SCREAM, Rowland et al., 2016;RivMAP, Schwenk et al., 2017;PyRIS, Monegaglia et al., 2018). Combining these techniques and approaches, it is possible to assess river channel change over larger spatial extents and at finer temporal resolutions than ever before (Boothroyd et al., 2021b).

In this paper, we use several sources of satellite data to monitor morphological adjustments along a 46 km reach of the Yamuna River. The study site is anthropogenically stressed, with flow regulated by the Dakpathar and Hathni Kund Barrages and the actions of sediment mining activities. The implication is that the Yamuna River has now moved into a situation where the natural driving hydrological processes are secondary to combined impacts of human stress via dams and mining. Such a situation is likely common across the region yet remains largely unquantified. The primary aim of this paper is thus to meet this challenge by analysing the morphological adjustments to these stresses. To meet this aim the specific objectives of this paper include, 1) delineation of the active river channel using a threshold-based approach from multi-spectral indices, for each year with satellite data available. 2) Based on output from objective 1, quantification of morphological change using the reach averaged width, accretional and erosional areas, and centreline migration rates. 3) Using additional information on precipitation, discharge, flow regulation, and details of sediment mining, identify the possible underlying controls on the morphological regime of the Yamuna River. 4) Finally, we evaluate the concept of stasis relating to the observed lateral channel dynamics, considering the general trend of the monsoon, and potential scenarios of flow regulation, which suggests the stabilization of the river in the recent years. Based on the satellite-derived observations and geomorphic interpretations, we suggest future measures that can inform sustainable river management activities.

div.head: Study area
div.p: The Yamuna River is the largest tributary of the Ganga, which originates from the Yamunotri Glacier, flows through the high Himalayan ranges, exiting the Himalayas near Dehradun, then flows through the National Capital Region, Delhi. A large population resides on the banks of the Yamuna River as it passes through the historical cities of Dehradun (1.69 million), Delhi (16.78 million), Mathura (2.54 million) and Agra (4.41 million) (Census of India, 2011). The Yamuna River is a valuable water resource for domestic and agricultural purposes, an economic construction material (sand and gravel), freshwater habitat, and many recreational activities in north India. It delivers nearly 125 Mt/year of sediment at Prayagraj before joining the Ganga (Sinha et al., 2005). Erosion of the high Himalayan mountains acts as a major source of sediment in north Indian rivers. We focus on a segment of the Yamuna River (~ 46 km) from the Dakpathar Barrage to the Tajewala Barrage as shown in Figure 1. The segment was selected for its location immediately downstream of the mountain front where alterations to the flow regime and sediment supply from natural and anthropogenic stresses will be directly reflected.

We briefly overview the stream network and catchment properties (section 2.1), geology (section 2.2), climate (section 2.3), history of flow regulation (section 2.4) and provide context for sediment mining activities in the region (section 2.5).

div.head: Catchment description
div.p: The Yamuna catchment is located in the north-western Himalayan ranges in Uttarakhand, and Himanchal Pradesh in India (Figure 1). Stream network and catchment properties of the Yamuna are shown in Table 1. At the Dakpathar Barrage, the Yamuna drains an area of ~7500 km 2 . The catchment headwaters are mainly glaciated and bounded by the Greater Himalayan ranges with a maximum elevation of 6281 m. The river flow at Tajewala is of a similar magnitude to that of Bhagirathi and Alaknanda (Dalai et al., 2002), which joins to form the Ganga, and is characterised by steep terrain and high relief. The mean catchment slope is 30°, with 90% of the catchment area lying above 1271 m, and 10% above 4074 m. The stream network mainly flows in a north to south direction with a mean slope of 0.14 m/m. Further, the catchment is mainly dominated with agricultural and forest areas, with glaciers located in the northern region (Figure S2). The proportion of agricultural area has increased over the time, with other land use classes approximately consistent (Figure S3).

div.head: Geology
div.p: The selected segment is composed of alluvial deposits, with bed surface forms consisting of sand with some traces of fine gravel. However, based on the geologic classification, the segment falls in the category of Siwaliks (partly faulted and folded Sub-Himalayan Molasse units) (Srivastava and Mitra, 1994). In the upper parts of the catchment, the inverted metamorphic geology mainly characterizes the bedrock geology, which is typically found throughout the mountains (Vannay et al., 2004;Yin, 2006).

div.head: Climate
div.p: The region experiences two atmospheric circulations, the southwest Indian Summer Monsoon during July-October (4 months), and westerlies during winters in December-January (Bookhagen and Burbank, 2010;Wulf et al., 2010). Lower regions of the catchment experience an annual rainfall of nearly 2500 mm/year with higher regions ranging between 1000-2500 mm/year (Bookhagen and Burbank, 2010). With increasing elevation values above 3000 m, rainfall decreases and snowfall increases (Wulf et al., 2010). Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) based gridded precipitation shows a catchment averaged precipitation of 1122 mm over the last 30 years.

div.head: History of flow regulation
div.p: The annual water discharge at the Tajewala Barrage (decommissioned now, replaced with Hathnikund Barrage in 1999) was 342.46 m 3 /sec (Dalai et al., 2002;Jha et al., 1988). Currently there are two dams in the Yamuna catchment, the Ichari Dam (Gross storage capacity = 8.9
Mm 3 ) completed in 1972, and the larger Lakhwar-Vyasi Dam (Gross storage capacity = 580

Mm 3 ), completed in 2017 as shown in Figure 1. Initially, the construction of Lakhwar-Vyasi Dam started in 1987, but stopped in 1992 at nearly 30% completion due to environmental issues. In 2008, this project was notified as a project of national importance and received environmental clearance from the Ministry of Environment and Forest. The construction of the dam started in 2013 and was completed in 2017; currently it is the largest operating dam in the Yamuna catchment. Furthermore, the Dakpathar Barrage (started operation in 1965) and Tajewala Barrage (operating since 1873 and decommissioned in 1999) are located further downstream; the segment under consideration is located between these two barrages (Figure 1). In 1999, the Tajewala Barrage was replaced by Hathni Kund Barrage located slightly upstream of it. Moreover, a power canal starting from Dakpathar Barrage, runs nearly parallel to the Yamuna River, passing through Asan Barrage Bird Sanctuary and re-joins the Yamuna River at Hathni Kund Barrage. The river segment between Dakpathar and Hathni Kund Barrage acts as a natural border between the states of Haryana and Himachal Pradesh.

div.head: Sediment mining in the Yamuna River segment
div.p: Sand and gravel extracted from rivers is largely used as a construction material in India, attracting illegal sand mining activities in the region. Recently, India ranked second in the use of construction sand, a dwindling and increasing valuable resource (UNEP, 2019). However, sand and gravel are a basic construction material, and the global demand is around 50 billion tonnes a day (Gallagher and Peduzzi, 2019). Recently, there has been an increased incidence of illegal sand and gravel mining on the Yamuna River (Rawat, 2021;Singh and Kumar, 2018), which may have consequences for the hydrological and morphological regime. Although sand mining is regulated by certain rules and regulations from the government of India (Ministry of Mines, 2018a, 2018b), the region is often subject to illegal sediment mining activities (Rege, 2016).

div.head: Rainfall and river discharge estimates
div.p: Indian Meteorological Data (IMD) gridded rainfall product, available from 1901 at 0.25 o * 0.25 o spatial resolution (https://cdsp.imdpune.gov.in/home_gridded_data.php) was used to estimate catchment averaged statistics on rainfall. This gridded dataset was developed using rainfall observations from 6955 rain gauge stations in India, followed by Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) interpolation (Jena et al., 2020;Pai et al., 2014). Each grid cell is deemed as a proxy of the rain gauge station, the rainfall value of which is obtained using the interpolation of the nearest rain gauge stations.

In the absence of observed discharge, the mean daily river flow at the Hathni Kund Barrage was extracted using the simulated GloFAS (Global Flood Awareness System) historical products (Harrigan et al., 2020), and global WBMsed (Cohen et al., 2022). Both GloFAS and
WBMsed have been proven to be reliable and can reproduce well the magnitude and seasonality of the flow (Cohen et al., 2013;Harrigan et al., 2020;Senent-Aparicio et al., 2021;Zăinescu et al., 2023).

div.head: River planform mapping from optical satellite imagery
div.p: Google Earth Engine (GEE) was used to extract information on river planform from multitemporal, multi-spectral satellite imagery. Landsat surface reflectance products (Landsat 5

Thematic Mapper, Landsat 7 Enhanced Thematic Mapper and Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager) acquired from 1989 to 2021 were the primary sources of satellite data, with most spectral bands having a spatial resolution of 30 m. A region of interest that represents the selected segment was first defined. Following Boothroyd et al., (2021a), all available Landsat images for one-year time periods were selected for analysis, the CFmask algorithm was applied to mask obstructions from cloud and cloud shadow pixels (Foga et al., 2017) and a median reducer was applied to generate a temporal composite image. The temporal composite image represents an "average" image for each calendar year, containing pixel-wide information for each of the spectral bands.

Temporal composite images were used to calculate multi-spectral indices, including the Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI; Xu, 2006) and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI; Rouse et al., 1974). Multi-spectral indices are useful for identifying features of interest in fluvial environments (Spada et al., 2018). The threshold-based approach of Boothroyd et al., (2021c) was modified and used to classify the active river channel. The active river channel includes both the wetted channels and exposed unvegetated sediment deposits. The active channel was classified using a pixel-wide relational operator such that MNDWI > -0.5 and NDVI < 0.15. A minimum threshold of 50 connected pixels was adopted to omit disconnected pixels not connected to the channel. Although an NDVI threshold of 0.2 has been previously applied to indicate dense riparian vegetation (Bertoldi et al., 2011), the NDVI threshold was lowered here due to the reduced vegetation coverage in the Himalayan setting. Water pixels were identified where MNDWI > 0 and the remaining non-water pixels were classified as exposed sediment. Binary images for the active river channel were generated for each year with satellite data available. Information on number of water-pixels and exposed sediment-pixels were also extracted.
A second source of satellite data used to extend the analysis further back in time was declassified CORONA satellite imagery, with stereo medium camera resolution (USGS, 1996).

Available image tiles from 1965, 1973 and 1976 provided historical insights on active river channels. Images were georeferenced using more than 100 known ground control points (GCPs). A third order polynomial transformation was used with a nearest neighbour resampling method, which yielded a mean error ranging between 6.23 to 11.19 m for different image tiles, comparable with accuracy statistics reported elsewhere (Iacone et al., 2022). The georeferenced CORONA satellite imagery was manually digitized using QGIS software to delineate the active channel where surface water and non-vegetated alluvial surfaces were observed, using the riparian vegetation limit (after Gurnell (1997)). The active channel outputs were rasterized to a 30 m spatial resolution in order to make the spatial resolution comparable to the outputs from Landsat imagery.
High-resolution aerial imagery from Google Earth was used for the years 2011, 2015 and 2021

to check outputs from the optical satellite imagery-based analysis. The active channel was manually digitized from the aerial imagery, followed by rasterization to a 30 m spatial resolution in order to make it comparable with the outputs from the Landsat and CORONA imagery.

div.head: Mean width and annual centreline migration
div.p: The segment of the Yamuna River under consideration mainly exhibited a single-thread channel, with very few bars. The braiding index (BI*), calculated as the ratio of area of bars to active channel area of segment reach (Das and Islam, 2023) changed from 0.22 in 1989 to 0.11 in 2021. The mean active channel width and centreline was extracted using the MATLABbased RivMAP (River Morphodynamics from Analysis of Planforms) toolbox (Schwenk et al., 2017). RivMAP allows the determination of the centreline from the input binary channel mask and is suitable for the analysis of planform characteristics in single-thread channels. In the case of multi-thread channels having large bars or secondary channels, the centreline determined would be relative to the banklines, irrespective of regions between the channel threads. The approach adequately represents centreline dynamics, with changes in the binary active channel used to identify zones of erosion and deposition. We extracted the effective channel width, determined by dividing the active channel area by the centreline length. Further, the migration rate was determined by dividing the migrated area by the centreline length. The same approach was used to extract the effective channel width for the outputs from CORONA and Google Earth imagery.

div.head: Catchment-averaged rainfall and river discharge estimates
div.p: Total annual rainfall ranged from 1258 mm in 1990 to 1280 mm in 2021 based on the IMD gridded rainfall. Catchment-averaged annual rainfall based on the daily Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) gridded data was observed to be 1122 mm for the last 32 years for the Yamuna catchment. Further, the daily mean (standard deviation = 0.67 mm), maximum (standard deviation = 20 mm), and 95 th percentile (standard deviation = 4 mm) of rainfall averaged over the catchment appeared consistent with changes in mean annual rainfall (Figure 2). Trends in rainfall over the time period 1990 to 2021 were calculated using the Sen slope.

Results indicate overall trends in rainfall for the period, in addition to some spatial variability in rainfall trends across the catchment (Figure S1). Averaged over the catchment, total annual rainfall (S = 0.05 mm/year), mean daily rainfall (S = 0.001 mm/year) and 95 th percentile daily rainfall (S = 0.02 mm/year) increased. The maximum daily rainfall decreased (S = -0.11 mm/year). Overall, the catchment averaged trends in rainfall show no significant change over the analysis period.

Mean annual daily river discharge at the Hathni Kund Barrage estimated from GloFAS and WBMsed models were similar for both models (Figure 3). However, the annual maximum discharge and 95 th percentile of daily discharge varies in magnitude between models. GloFAS discharge most closely resembled the IMD observed rainfall, showing higher discharges for the higher rainfall years. The effects of flow regulation are not represented within the GloFAS model as it is based on the ERA-5 reanalysis product. Although WBMsed considers flow regulation effects using the global dam database; GranD v1.3 (Lehner et al., 2011), no dams or barrages are represented within the Yamuna catchment. Therefore, the river discharge estimates do not explicitly represent flow regulation effects within the catchment.

div.head: Morphological adjustments of the active channel
div.p: Active channel masks obtained from optical satellite imagery and aerial imagery reveal the complex and active morphodynamics of the Yamuna River. Overall, the active channel remained in quasi-equilibrium from 1989 to 2013 (a balance between narrowing and widening), but underwent substantial narrowing after 2013 (Figure 4 and5). This narrowing trend was distributed along the whole segment length, with the planform adjusting towards a single-thread channel. From the historical CORONA images (1965, 1973, and 1976), river planform was similar to that of the 1990s in terms of segment averaged width, and other morphological factors. Further, Figure 6 Segment averaged active channel width has decreased over the analysis period (Figure 5). Multi-spectral imagery is used to separate surface water pixels from exposed sediment pixels using an MNDWI threshold, to explore internal changes within the active channel over the analysis period. Inter-annual variation in the segment averaged surface water and exposed sediment area within the active channel is shown in Figure 6a. The surface water area remains approximately constant over the analysis period 1989 to 2021 (mean = 5.89 km 2 , standard deviation = 1.12 km 2 ), with no abrupt changes through time. The exposed sediment area gradually decreases from 1989 to 2010 but decreases more steeply from 2011 onwards. Where the surface water area remains approximately constant, the reduction in area of exposed sediment is responsible for reducing the overall area of the active channel. The proportion of the active channel consisting of exposed sediment was substantial from 1989 to 2010, accounting for ~80% of the total area (Figure 6b). By 2021, the proportion has decreased to ~50%, indicating internal changes whereby surface waters are covering relatively more of the active channel area.

div.head: Erosional-accretional areas within the active channel
div.p: The active channel exhibits complex patterns of erosion and accretion (Figure 7). Taking the end-points of the Landsat imagery analysis period between 1989 and 2021, the overall erosional (0.61 km 2 ) and accretional (8.08 km 2 ) areas reveal that accretion has been greater than erosion. There has been a cumulative loss of floodplain area over the analysis period, but this does not provide information on the spatio-temporal patterns of erosion and accretion during the intervening period.

Erosional and accretional areas were assessed at decadal intervals to reveal changes during the intervening period (Figure 7). From 1991 to 2001, the study reach experiences both erosion and accretion, with the erosional area (3.01 km 2 ) nearly half that of the accretional area (6.03 km 2 ). Spatially, accretion is mainly located in the upstream part of the reach, with erosion positioned further downstream. From 2001 to 2011, similar patterns of erosion and accretion were observed in the reach (erosion = 2.59 km 2 and accretion = 5.72 km 2 ). Before 2011, the reach was laterally mobile; evidencing areas of erosion and accretion that resulted in active channel expansion and narrowing. From 2011 to 2021, the reach was dominated by accretion, with considerably less erosion (erosion = 0.53 km 2 and accretion = 12.68 km 2 ). This causes a net imbalance of reworked floodplain, despite some local erosion and accretion. After 2011, the increase in accretion led to substantial narrowing of the active channel. Comparisons of erosion and accretion at decadal intervals indicate that the reach was in a quasi-equilibrium state from 1991 to 2011, thereafter switching to a strongly accretion dominated state with minor evidence of erosion concentrated locally.

div.head: Centreline migration of the active channel
div.p: Positional changes of the active channel centreline from 1989 to 2021 indicates considerable dynamism of the Yamuna River (Figure 8). Comparing the centreline positions at the endpoints of the analysis period (1989 and 2021), a migration rate of 5.88 m/year is calculated over 32 years. However, when centreline migration is annually resolved (i.e., calculated for each of the 28 years with data available), the mean centreline migration rate was 34.63 m/year.

This difference of nearly one order of magnitude is likely due to compensation between erosion and accretion during the intervening years. Using annually resolved centreline data, specific years of interest can be further investigated. In 2010, the catchment-averaged annual rainfall total was 1860 mm; this was the highest recorded total between 1989 and 2021. For the same year, the annually resolved centreline migration rate (45.51 m/year) was the highest recorded, 31% higher than the mean centreline migration rate and indicative of the control of extreme rainfall on active channel dynamism.

With the centreline migration analysis repeated at decadal intervals, end-point analysis provided migration rates of 9.52 m/year for 1991-2001, 5.74 m/year for 2001-2011 and 12.9 m/year for 2011-2021. Using annually resolved centreline data for the same decades, the mean centreline migration rates were 39.65 m/year, 32.86 m/year and 31.04 m/year, comparable with the annually resolved mean centreline migration rate over the entire analysis period. Again, the differences in centreline migration rates suggest compensation between erosion and accretion in the intervening years.

div.head: Sediment mining within the active channel
div.p: Google Earth imagery from 2011, 2015 and 2021 shows an increasing incidence of sediment mining scars within the active channel over the last decade (Figure 9). Three locations were selected to manually digitize sediment mining scars and infer mining activity. The first location is at the upstream end of the river segment, located downstream of the Dakpathar Barrage Himanchal Pradesh (g-i). 10). The first reach can be assumed to be explicitly affected by flow regulation with minimal mining, while the other is due to combined effects of sediment mining and flow regulation.

The inter-annual variation in the surface water and exposed sediment area of both reaches exhibit a rather similar narrowing pattern after 2013. However, narrowing was rather gradual in the first reach impacted by flow regulation and more rapid in the case of the second reach, corroborating the combined effects of flow regulation and sediment mining. This shows that the combined effects of both processes will result in rapid morphologic changes. Estimating the quantitative effects of sediment mining and flow regulation separately poses significant challenges, and the analysis primarily provides qualitative (subjective) impacts of both processes. Future studies could be directed toward addressing this challenge.

div.head: Stasis in the active channel
div.p: River systems are conceptualised to be composed of floodplain (excluding channel belt), channel belt (excluding channel) and the channel; this conceptualisation is used to estimate the first order stasis of the system. If the area occupied by the floodplain (excluding channel belt), channel belt (excluding channel), and channel itself are Af, Acb, Ac, and the corresponding average time proportion of stasis are tf, tcb, and tc, respectively (Figure 11), the first order estimate of the system as a whole can be given by: !𝐴 ! * 𝑡 ! % + (𝐴 "# * 𝑡 "# ) + (𝐴 " * 𝑡 " ). Bridge (2003) suggested the proportion of area for Af, Acb, and Ac to be 0.95, 0.04, 0.01. Further, Tipper (2015) suggested the time proportion of stasis tf, tcb, and, tc to be 0.99, 0.90, and 0.1, respectively. A tf of 0.99 for the floodplain suggests flood supplied sediment to be deposited only 1% of time; tcb of 0.90 suggest flood supplied sediment to be deposited only 10% of time in the channel belt (nearly around one month in a year), and tc of 0.1 suggests erosion and deposition occurs during 90% of the time everywhere in the channel. Only 10% of the time does the channel remain in stasis. Here we consider different values for the time proportion of stasis as the river flow is dominated by the strong monsoon, which lasts for nearly 4 months. We assume that the maximum time flooding may occur over the entire floodplain causing erosion/deposition is one month, and over the channel belt is four months (whole monsoon). Thus, in accordance with these assumptions, we adopt the time proportion of stasis tf, tcb, and tc for the unregulated river to be 0.90, 0.70, and 0.10, respectively considering the characteristic of the Indian Monsoon. This corresponds to 10% of the time that flood supplied sediment can be deposited on the floodplain (nearly one full month), 30% of the time that flood supplied sediment can be deposited in the channel belt (nearly 4 months), and 90% of the time that erosion/deposition can occur everywhere in the channel. With these assumptions for the unregulated river, the proportion of stasis in the system is estimated to be 0.88. For 88% of the time the river system will be in stasis and erosion/deposition can only occur 12% of the time.

Extending this modified example, flow regulation effects due to dams and barrages will reduce flood peaks; whereby studies have shown reduction in peak flows by nearly 80% and median flows by nearly 50% as compared to pre-dam flows (Burbano et al., 2020;FitzHugh and Vogel, 2011;Puttock et al., 2021;Zahar et al., 2008). The reduction in peak flows disconnects the floodplain from the channel, reducing the likelihood of flooding and sediment deposition on the floodplain and resulting in stasis for longer durations. If the time proportion of stasis for the floodplains increases to 0.95 (compared to 0.90 in the previous case) due to flow regulation effects, keeping the other factors unchanged, the time proportion of stasis for the entire channel increases to 0.93 compared to 0.88 for the case of the unregulated river. A further increase in the stasis time proportion for the floodplain to 0.99 will render the entire river system to be in stasis for a longer proportion, increasing the channel stasis to 0.96. Rivers regulated by dams are forced into a state where the system remains in stasis, doing nothing for longer durations as compared to unregulated rivers. In this anthropogenically stressed state, the system tends to remain stable and the floodplain can be abandoned completely.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: This work investigated the spatio-temporal dynamics of the Yamuna River in the Himalayan foothills in response to natural and anthropogenic stresses. As shown in section 4.2, the river has undergone substantial narrowing in the last decade, more specifically after 2013, which may further impact the morphological functioning. This abrupt narrowing of the river indicates the strong influence of anthropogenic stresses, rather than the natural controls, and coincides with the construction of the Lakhwar-Vyasi Dam. Change in the active channel width could be related to the alterations in the sediment supply from higher Himalayan mountains due to flow regulation, deposition of which controls the morphology of the river in lower reaches. The sediment carried by the river, along with flow from upstream regions, are a major cause of changes in river planform and active channel width (Best, 1988). The construction of dams/reservoirs acts as a sedimentation basin causing reduced fine sediment supply to downstream reaches (Kondolf, 1995;Kondolf et al., 2014). Moreover, coarse sediment can be trapped upstream of dams (Moran et al., 2018), which abrades during selective transport to produce finer sediment grains and feed downstream reaches.

Anthropogenic modifications to river flow or sediment supply due to urbanisation, land use changes, dams, diversions, gravel and sand mining, can have serious implications on the river dynamics (Surian and Rinaldi, 2003). Reductions in bedload transport due to changes in population pressures, reforestation and the construction of check dams (Boix-Fayos et al., 2008;Kondolf et al., 2002;Liébault and Piégay, 2001) impart a major control on river morphology, leading to river narrowing and decreasing braiding index (Ashmore, 1991). On the contrary, increases in bedload supply generally leads to widened and aggraded channel (Kondolf et al., 2002). In the Yamuna catchment, the construction of the Lakhwar-Vyasi Dam restarted in 2013 (after being stopped in 1998 at 30% completion); this likely trapped a significant portion of sediment from upstream, causing downstream reaches to become sediment starved, similar to the observations of Schmidt and Wilcock (2008) in several rivers in the western United States.

Our centreline migration analyses indicated the considerable dynamism for the study reach of the Yamuna River. For the analysis period 1989-2021, our results showed differences in the migration rates between annually resolved centrelines (mean average = 34.63 m/year), and endpoint analyses (5.88 m/year, between 1989 and 2021). This nearly one order of magnitude higher migration rate for the annually resolved centrelines, compared to end-point analysis,

indicates the active dynamism with centreline shifting towards both banks during intermediate alternative years, rather than a trend of shifting in one particular direction. Although the differences are probably due to compensation occurring between erosional-accretional areas during the intermediate interval, the differences highlight the importance of selecting an appropriate time interval for centreline migration analysis in morphological applications.

Further, the highest centreline migration rates were associated with the highest rainfall years (i.e., 2010), the migration rates were nearly 30% higher than the mean annually resolved migration rate, indicating the control of extreme flow events on morphological change.

Extreme flood and rainfall events have a major impact on channel morphology (Akay et al., 2022). In future applications, the use of aerial or satellite imagery with a higher spatio-temporal resolution may provide further insights into event-scale morphodynamics (Akay et al., 2020;Schwenk et al., 2017).

Increasing mining activities in the last decade have likely enhanced the imbalance between sand/gravel extraction and sediment supply from upstream. Mining scars, in the sediment starved reach, which would likely have been replenished with sediment in an unregulated river, can lead to the abandonment of portions of the active channel. The abandoned part of the active channel leads to active channel narrowing. Sand mining is evident even before 2011, but scars can be filled by sediment supplied from upstream causing the morphology to be restored. The continuous narrowing of the reach after 2014 coincides with the combined stresses of extensive mining and flow regulation, causing reduced sediment supply that limits the capacity for scars to be filled. Similar narrowing patterns have been observed on the Reno River (Italy) in response to gravel mining and flow regulation (Preciso et al., 2012). Furthermore, Shields Jr et al., (2000) showed that channel stabilization, and reduction in peak flows due to flow regulation on the Missouri River has disconnected the floodplains from the channel, leading to reduced channel migration rates. However, quantification of explicit effects of flow regulation and sediment mining in deriving morphological changes poses significant challenges, and can be explored in future studies.

The narrowing trend in active channel width after 2013, reduction in annually resolved centreline migration rate in last decade (i.e., 31.04 m/year for 2011-2021, compared to 39.65 m/year during 1991-2001), and dominance of an accretional regime (Figure 7) suggests that the Yamuna River is becoming more stable and single threaded. Although the river mainly exhibits a single-thread channel, the braiding index changed from 0.22 in 1989 to 0.11 in 2021, confirming the observation of channel stabilisation. This increases floodplain area which is no longer undergoing frequent episodes of flooding owing to increased stasis (Tipper, 2015). The reduction in peak flows due to flow regulation acts to disconnect the floodplain (and even the channel belt), increasing the proportion of time that the river system is in stasis, consequently leading to the abandonment of parts of the floodplain. This eventually leads to channel narrowing and reduced migration rates, in accordance with Ward and Stanford (1995). These morphological effects may have broader ecological implications, including negative impacts on biodiversity due to changing habitat because of abandoned bars, and floodplains (Fox, 1979). The intermediate disturbance hypothesis suggests a sweet spot of biodiversity due to the rich mosaic of habitat types incorporating those that turnover rapidly all the way through to those that turnover infrequently. Channel stabilisation and narrowing may render the river system to a state where habitat turns over infrequently, leading to a loss of biodiversity.

Further, the government of India has planned 292 new hydropower dams throughout the Indian Himalayas, with an aim to double the hydropower capacity contributing 6% of the total projected energy needs by 2030 (Grumbine and Pandit, 2013). Out of the 292, a large portion belongs to the north-western Himalayas in the Ganga River basin, and 21 hydropower dams are planned in the Yamuna catchment (Pandit and Grumbine, 2012). The completion of these hydropower projects will fulfil the energy needs of the nation but may have serious consequences for river morphology and ecology. It is likely that additional anthropogenic stresses would compound the negative impacts on the morphodynamics of the Yamuna River, as demonstrated in this study.

The Lakhwar-Vyasi Dam may have trapped coarse sediment from upstream, leading to reduced sediment supply in downstream reaches, affecting the equilibrium between the sediment supply and extraction. Dam reservoirs often act as a sedimentation basin, retaining a major part of finer fraction apart from coarse sediment (Kondolf, 1995;Kondolf et al., 2014;Wisser et al., 2013). Increased sediment mining activities in the last decade, and a reduction in the sediment supply downstream due to trapping upstream, coincides with the narrowing pattern of the river segment. The sediment trapped upstream of the dam may have downstream consequences on river morphology, affecting the sedimentary and geomorphic units (Assani and Petit, 2004;Phillips et al., 2005;Yang et al., 2014). The cumulative effects of anthropogenic stresses from flow regulation and mining will have consequences for the morphological regime of Yamuna River. Likewise, the location of mining activities near to dams, barrages, bridges and other infrastructure may pose additional hazards. Based on these findings, site-specific flow regulations and sediment management strategies for the Yamuna River can be recommended as:
• The hydrological and morphological regime should to be monitored to track future adjustments to natural and anthropogenic stresses; helping inform sustainable river management policies.

• Minimum environmental flows should be ensured to maintain the natural flow and regime of the river. Moreover, the possible high flows should be released through the dams a couple of times a year, to maintain the channel width and restore any changes within the morphological regime of the river (including floodplain and channel belt).

• Mining activities should be prohibited in the close vicinity of hydraulic structures including dams, barrages, and bridge infrastructures as the bed degradation exposes foundations to the flow, which can compromise the safety of the infrastructure.

• River gravel and sand act as a key construction material in India, and a complete ban might lead to imbalance in construction industry and compromise national development. However, mining activities can be regulated by limiting to certain periods of the year, preferably before the monsoon. The relatively higher flows during the monsoon may replenish sediment, maintaining a balance between gravel/sand needs and riverine ecology.
• A tribunal might be formed other than the Ministry of Mines, Government of India to mark a check in the mining activities without compromising with the natural riverine flow and morphology.

div.head: Limitations of this study
div.p: This work is primarily based on the analysis of satellite-based imagery. Active channel pixels were classified using relational operators where MNDWI ≥ -0.5 and NDVI ≤ 0.15. The thresholds were shown to be suitable for the Himalayan setting by manually varying the MNDWI and NDVI threshold values and cross-verifying active channel extents using Google Earth imagery. If applied to other geographical settings, the relational operators for active channel pixels may need to be modified due to differences in the vegetation density (e.g., Bertoldi et al. (2011) used an NDVI threshold of 0.2 in the Tagliamento River (Italy) to differentiate dense vegetation). It should be noted that any significant changes in the reflectance characteristics of the region might also lead to varying MNDWI and NDVI thresholds with time. Here, we assumed that the reflectance characteristics did not change over the analysis period. A critical relationship exists between the width of the river and the spatial resolution of the satellite imagery suitable for analysis (Boothroyd et al., 2021b). The segment of the Yamuna River was characterised by widths > 250 m, meaning that Landsat data with a 30 m spatial resolution should adequately resolve the active river channel. However, as noted by Gilvear and Bryant (2016), an unquantified source of uncertainty arises where satellite imagery pixel edges do not coincide with the edges of river objects (e.g., water, exposed sediment and vegetation). In a temporal context, the use of annually resolved temporal composite images reduced the risk that short-term changes (e.g., variation in water stage) would be misrepresented as morphological change. In doing so, we assumed that the response to extreme flood events would be visible in this annually resolved imagery. The above considerations enabled changes in river morphology to be assessed over the analysis period.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Our investigation quantified morphological adjustments along a 46 km reach of the Yamuna River in the Himalayan foothills. Active channel changes were quantified from Landsat satellite imagery between 1989 to 2021, using an NDVI and MNDWI threshold-based approach. Declassified CORONA satellite imagery and high-resolution Google Earth aerial imagery provided longer term insights into historical river channel change. We found that the observed morphological adjustments coincided with key anthropogenic stresses (namely flow regulation and sediment mining). The major conclusions are summarised as:

• The active channel exhibited complex patterns of erosion and accretion. Comparisons of erosion and accretion at decadal intervals indicated that the segment was in a quasiequilibrium state from 1991 to 2011, thereafter switching to a strongly accretion dominated state. This was reflected in abrupt narrowing of the active channel width (~ 523 m in 2013 to 237 m in 2021).

• The proportion of the active channel consisting of exposed sediment was substantial from 1989 to 2010, accounting for ~80% of the total area. By 2021, the proportion had decreased to ~50%, indicating considerable changes in river morphology.

• Annually resolved centreline migration rates were estimated to be 34.63 m/year from 1989 to 2021. However, decadal migration rates of 39.65 m/year (1991-2001), 32.86 m/year (2001-2011), and 31.04 m/year (2011-2021) suggest that the river became more stable.

• Morphologic changes in the river after 2013 coincide with flow regulation due to the Lakhwar-Vyasi Dam. Flow regulation likely renders the floodplain and channel belt into stasis (a state of inactivity) for longer durations.

• Increases in mining activities in the last decade, in addition to the effects of flow regulation, compound the imbalances between sediment supply and extraction, contributing to further channel narrowing.

Many new dams are planned in the Yamuna catchment and elsewhere across India, additionally, there is currently very little quantification of sand mining activity, largely because of illegal extraction. Thus, important river management actions are taking place without the necessary data with which to make properly informed decisions of the combined impacts of these anthropogenic activities. Given that obtaining data from the field is time-consuming and expensive, it is unlikely this situation will improve without a different approach being taken.

A key application of this paper is therefore that remote sensing can generate the necessary baseline data quickly and easily using freely available platforms. Thus, the combined effects of human stresses via dams and mining can be more readily assessed. Therefore, the approach taken in this study may inform river strategists and authorities to plan and implement sustainable river action plans without compromising the river ecology as we enter a new era where human modification to the hydrological regime is becoming the dominant factor in driving the river morphology.
